passage: On a cold morning in Cape Town, Thabo and Lucia sat outside the ice-cream stand. Thabo rubbed his hands together, fast, eyes on the seller. Lucia snapped her fingers in time to the radio. “Are you cold or excited?” she asked. “Both,” said Thabo. “Hot chocolate!” He snapped his fingers at the seller. “Hey!” The seller frowned. Lucia winced. “Try ‘Excuse me’,” she whispered. Thabo went red. “Excuse me, please, could I have two hot chocolates?” The seller smiled slightly. “Coming up.”

qa.q: What did Lucia snap her fingers in time to?
qa.a: She snapped her fingers in time to the radio.

qa.q: Why was Thabo rubbing his hands together, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: He said he was both cold and excited, and his eyes were on the seller, so it was likely a mix of cold and eagerness for hot chocolate. Rubbing hands can mean either alone.

qa.q: What could Thabo try next time to get a seller's attention?
qa.a: Say “Excuse me, please” and wait for eye contact, as he did on the second try, rather than snapping.

qa.q: How might the seller have felt when Thabo snapped his fingers?
qa.a: Probably annoyed or disrespected, since he frowned. The seller relaxed when Thabo asked politely.

grounding: Snapping fingers and rubbing hands have different meanings depending on context, and snapping at people can seem rude.

passage: In the sports hall before the kabaddi match, Divyansh rubbed his hands together, fast, and bounced on his toes. The hall was cold, and he was also dying to start. “Eager or freezing?” his teammate Mohit teased. “Both!” Mohit snapped his fingers at the coach across the hall to get his attention. The coach looked over slowly. “I'm not a waiter, Mohit.” Mohit's face went hot. “Sorry, Coach. Could you tell us where to stand?” “Better. Left side, both of you.” Divyansh grinned and rubbed his hands again.

qa.q: Where did the coach tell Divyansh and Mohit to stand?
qa.a: He told them to stand on the left side.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh rubbing his hands, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: He was probably eager to start, and the cold hall could explain it too. He says it is both.

qa.q: What could Mohit do instead of snapping his fingers?
qa.a: Say “Coach” or “Sorry to interrupt” and ask his question politely, as he did on the second try.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt when Mohit snapped his fingers at him?
qa.a: Probably a bit annoyed, since he said he was not a waiter. He was happy when Mohit asked politely.

grounding: Snapping fingers and rubbing hands mean different things by context; snapping at people can seem rude.

passage: I'm Sonali, Imran's cousin, and I was at the dhaba with his family on Sunday. When the food was late, Imran snapped his fingers at the waiter twice, loudly, the way people do in films. The waiter's face went stiff, and he walked the other way. Imran's Abbu leaned over. “Beta, snapping at someone feels like calling a dog. Say ‘Bhaiya, excuse me.’” Imran went red and nodded. Later, when the parathas came, he rubbed his hands together fast, grinning. The same waiter smiled at that. I think it looked hungry, not rude.

qa.q: How many times did Imran snap his fingers at the waiter?
qa.a: Imran snapped his fingers at the waiter twice.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he went red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, realising his snap had seemed rude when he only meant to get attention.

qa.q: What did Abbu suggest instead of snapping?
qa.a: He suggested saying “Bhaiya, excuse me,” a polite way to get the waiter's attention.

qa.q: How did the waiter likely feel about the snapping?
qa.a: The waiter probably felt disrespected, as if called rudely, which is why his face went stiff.

grounding: Shows a child snapping fingers to call attention, which seems rude at people, and rubbing hands in eager anticipation.

passage: Monday: During the maths test, Yash snapped his fingers under the desk, soft and steady, counting. Sahil, beside him, hissed, “Stop showing off!” Yash stopped, confused. Wednesday: At break, Yash explained. “The snaps help me count times tables. I wasn't doing it at you.” Sahil shrugged. “It just sounded like hurry up.” They agreed on a tap on the knee instead. Friday: A freezing morning. Sahil sat rubbing his hands together fast, grinning as the teacher handed out the quiz. Yash leaned over. “Cold, or excited?” “Both! I studied all week,” Sahil whispered.

qa.q: What did Yash and Sahil agree on instead of snapping?
qa.a: Yash and Sahil agreed on a tap on the knee instead.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Sahil hissed at him?
qa.a: Yash felt confused and a bit hurt, since the snapping was only to help count, not aimed at Sahil.

qa.q: What small step fixed Monday's problem?
qa.a: Explaining the snaps and agreeing on a quiet knee tap let Yash keep counting without it sounding like hurry up.

qa.q: How did the snapping sound to Sahil on Monday?
qa.a: To Sahil it sounded like showing off or telling him to hurry up, not like counting.

grounding: Shows finger-snapping as rhythm being misread, and hand-rubbing carrying both cold and eager anticipation.

passage: Jatin, stop snapping at your sister and listen to your Rukmini Paati. When I was nine, in our village music class, a boy named Selvam snapped his fingers all through the song. Snap, snap, snap. The teacher spun round and hit the desk with her ruler. “Are you calling me like a servant?” Selvam's face went grey. He whispered, “No, Teacher. It's how I keep the beat. My father keeps time that way for his drum students.” The teacher stopped. She asked him to snap again, slowly, while we sang. We all sang in time for the first time that year. After that she let him keep the beat, but never at people.

qa.q: What was Selvam doing all through the song?
qa.a: Selvam snapped his fingers all through the song.

qa.q: What was Selvam feeling when his face went grey?
qa.a: He felt frightened and shocked that his rhythm-keeping was taken as rudeness.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make after Selvam explained, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She asked him to snap slowly while the class sang, which turned a misunderstanding into help with the beat.

qa.q: How did the snapping first seem to the teacher?
qa.a: To the teacher it seemed like calling her rudely, like calling a servant, until she heard it was keeping time.

grounding: Shows finger-snapping as rhythm-keeping being mistaken for rudeness, and snapping at people being seen as rude.

passage:
The heater in the school hall had broken, and band practice started in coats. Baljeet rubbed his hands together hard, blowing into them between songs. When the drum part began, he snapped his fingers in rhythm, tapping one foot.

Then he lost his page. He turned and snapped his fingers twice at Nikita. "Sheet! Quick!"

Nikita raised an eyebrow. "I'm not a waiter."

Baljeet's ears went hot. "Sorry, sorry. Could you pass the sheet, please?" She passed it.

At the break, the cook brought in a tray of hot samosas, and Baljeet rubbed his hands again, grinning this time. Nikita laughed. "Is that cold hands or samosa hands?"
"Both!"

qa.q: Why did band practice start in coats?
qa.a: The heater in the school hall had broken.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he rubbed his hands at the break?
qa.a: Eager and excited about the hot samosas, as his grin shows, though his hands were probably still cold too, as he admits with "Both!".

qa.q: What could Baljeet do instead of snapping when he needs something quickly?
qa.a: Use the person's name and a quick "please", as he did after apologising.

qa.q: How did Nikita see the finger snap?
qa.a: She took it as rude, like calling a waiter, and felt annoyed until Baljeet said sorry and asked properly.

grounding: It shows a child snapping fingers in rhythm and to call someone, and rubbing hands from cold and eagerness, with the snap at a person coming across as rude.
